entries.ai_recommendation_summary: AI recommended always-on-sandbox, saying the team can connect immediately without any reservation and that safe read-only API practice fits a shared environment.
entries.rationale: The decisive requirement here is immediate access with no provisioning wait, which is exactly what an Always-On Sandbox is meant for. The Cisco sandbox documentation describes Always-On sandboxes as shared environments that are reachable right away and do not need to be reserved, and the scenario itself states that the team only needs safe read-only requests and no administrative changes. A Reservation Sandbox would technically work too, yet it would fail the one requirement that actually matters, which is that the team cannot wait for provisioning.

entries.ai_recommendation_summary: AI recommended reservation-sandbox, but it also claimed that every reservation sandbox always grants full administrator rights on every device in the pod.
entries.rationale: The decisive requirement is administrative control inside a private environment, and the scenario already accepts scheduling, VPN, and setup time, which are the exact trade-offs Cisco lists for this option. The sandbox documentation describes the Reservation Sandbox as a dedicated environment that is held for a block of time so the developer gets their own instance to configure, and that is what configuration testing needs. I marked this partially-verified because the privilege level is documented per individual sandbox rather than as one blanket guarantee, so the AI overstated it. An Always-On Sandbox was rejected for this case because it is shared and restricts administrative access, so configuration changes there would either fail or affect other users.

entries.ai_recommendation_summary: AI recommended learning-lab, however it added a claim that the labs hand the learner their own admin-level devices to keep after the lesson ends.
entries.rationale: The immediate need is guided, step-by-step content before the beginner attempts anything independently, and that is the stated role of DevNet Learning Labs on the Cisco learning page. I marked this partially-verified because the extra claim about keeping admin devices is not supported, and the module decision guide itself warns that Learning Labs are learning content and are not a substitute for choosing an execution environment. I still kept the selection as learning-lab because the scenario says the immediate goal is guided practice rather than access to administrative devices. Once the beginner moves on to the independent activity, a sandbox becomes the correct follow-up choice, but that is a later step and not this one.

entries.ai_recommendation_summary: AI first recommended always-on-sandbox so the developer could immediately browse and run automation code in a live environment.
entries.rationale: I rejected this recommendation because the AI answered a requirement that the scenario never asked for. The developer wants to examine existing community and Cisco-maintained repositories before designing anything, so the need is existing source code and not a device to execute it on. The Code Exchange page documents it as a curated index of community and Cisco-maintained repositories, which matches the scenario directly, and the module also notes that Automation Exchange has already been consolidated into Code Exchange. A sandbox would only become relevant later, after a repository is chosen and the code actually has to be reviewed and tested.
